note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Devon has just been made leading hand of a four-person electrical crew. Which of these is the main way he supports leadership on the job?
options: By doing all the hardest jobs himself so the crew can rest
By setting a good example and helping the crew meet the plan
By passing every question from the crew straight to the manager
By keeping the job plan to himself until each task begins

questions.stem: Why should a leading hand wear full PPE on site, even when he only goes in for a quick look at the work?
options: Because the crew copy what the leader does, not what he says
Because PPE is only checked when a supervisor is on the site
Because a leader is more likely to be hurt than the crew
Because the client pays extra when PPE is worn by leaders

questions.stem: Shanice sees Kemar about to change a light fitting without locking off the breaker. He says it will only take a minute. What should she do first?
options: Let him finish, then remind him at the next toolbox talk
Text the manager about it and carry on with her own work
Stop the work and have him isolate, lock off and prove dead
Stand guard by the breaker so that nobody switches it back on

questions.stem: A supplier offers Andre, the crew leader, a free phone if he orders all the job's cable from them. What is the best response?
options: Accept it, since the cable price is the same either way
Accept it, but share the phone with the rest of the crew
Accept it and say nothing, as it is a personal gift
Refuse it and tell his manager about the offer

questions.stem: Which action does most to build a crew's trust in their leader?
options: Taking the side of whichever worker has been there longest
Changing the rules each day so the crew stay alert
Doing what he said he would do, when he said he would
Keeping problems quiet so the crew do not worry

questions.stem: Tashana tells her leading hand that she has money problems and may need a day off. What should he do with this information?
options: Tell the crew so they understand why she is absent
Post a note on the site board so the manager can see it
Mention it at the toolbox talk as an example for others
Keep it private and discuss the day off with her alone

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a toolbox talk at the start of a shift?
options: To check who arrived late and record their pay deductions
To brief the crew on the day's tasks, hazards and controls
To let the client inspect the crew's tools before work starts
To give the leader time to finish the day's paperwork

questions.stem: After giving instructions for a cable pull, what is the best way for the leader to check that the crew understood?
options: Ask each member to say back their part in their own words
Ask the crew if there are any questions, then move on quickly
Repeat the same instructions a second time, more loudly
Hand out the instructions in writing and leave the site

questions.stem: The crew must choose between two cable routes through a building. Which step should come first in making a good decision?
options: Pick the route the leader used on the last job, as it worked then
Ask the manager to decide and wait for an answer
Choose the cheaper route without any more checks
Collect the facts: drawings, distances, costs and hazards

questions.stem: Why is it useful for a leading hand to ask the crew's views before deciding how to set out a job?
options: It means the leader is no longer responsible for the job's result
The crew often know practical problems the leader has missed
It is the only way to keep any job on time and on budget
It lets the leader blame the crew if anything goes wrong

questions.stem: Which task is best to delegate to Omar, a second-year apprentice, with supervision?
options: Fixing saddles along a conduit run that is already marked out
Signing the test certificate for the whole finished installation
Deciding the rating of the main breaker for the building
Agreeing a price for extra work with the client

questions.stem: After delegating a task, what should the leader do?
options: Leave the worker alone so they feel fully trusted
Do the same task over again himself to be sure it is right
Check progress at agreed points and give help if needed
Wait until the end of the job before looking at it

questions.stem: Kimone has fixed a run of conduit that is neat but not level. What is the best way to give her feedback?
options: Name what is good, show her the level problem, agree the fix
Tell the whole crew at lunch so they all learn from her mistake
Say nothing and quietly refix it after she has gone home
Tell her the work is poor and give the task to someone else

questions.stem: Which is the best way to recognise a crew member who found a serious fault before the client's handover?
options: Give him the easiest jobs for the rest of the month
Say nothing, because finding faults is part of his job
Thank him by name and tell the manager what he did
Let him leave early each day without telling anyone

questions.stem: Jermaine and Ricardo are arguing about whose turn it is to clean up the work area. What should the leader do first?
options: Tell them both to stop talking and do the work himself
Ask the manager to move one of them to a different job site
Let them sort it out alone, however long it takes
Listen to each side calmly, away from the rest of the crew

questions.stem: Which outcome is best when settling a dispute about work duties?
options: One person wins and the other is told to accept it
A fair rota that both agree to and the leader records
The leader decides and refuses to explain the reason
Both get a written warning so it does not happen again

questions.stem: The crew have worked long days to finish before a storm warning. Which action is most likely to keep them motivated?
options: Telling them that other crews work even longer hours
Explaining why the deadline matters and thanking them
Promising a bonus the leader has no power to give
Reminding them that they can be replaced if they complain

questions.stem: When mentoring an apprentice in how to terminate a cable, what is the best order?
options: Explain, show, let them try, then check and give feedback
Let them try first, then explain what they did wrong
Show it once quickly, then leave them to finish the board
Give them the manual and ask them to read it at home

questions.stem: A homeowner in Mandeville complains to the crew that they left dust on her furniture. What should the leader do?
options: Explain that dust is normal and cannot be avoided
Tell her to call the office, as the crew are busy
Apologise, clean it up, and use dust sheets from now on
Blame the plasterers who worked in the house the week before

questions.stem: Why does the way a crew dresses and speaks on a client's site matter to the company?
options: It decides which crew members are paid more each month
It only matters when the client is a large company
It is a legal duty written into every electrician's licence
Clients judge the company by what they see and hear

questions.stem: What should a leading hand use to check whether the crew's work meets the required standard?
options: How fast the crew finished the work compared with last week
What the most senior worker thinks looks right
The drawings, the specification and the quality checklist
Whether the client has noticed any problems yet

questions.stem: Marlon has arrived late four times this month. What is the best first step for his leader?
options: Report him to the manager and ask for him to be dismissed
Make a joke about it in front of the crew to shame him
Ignore it, because his work is good when he is there
Speak to him privately, find out why and agree a plan

questions.stem: The crew find that the drawing shows a socket outlet where a doorway now stands. What should the leader do?
options: Fit the outlet in the doorway, as the drawing shows
Hold that part, note the clash and ask the supervisor
Move it to any wall that looks right and tell nobody
Leave it out and hope the client does not notice

questions.stem: Which decision is usually within a leading hand's authority?
options: The order in which the crew do the day's tasks
Changing the price in the client's contract
Hiring a new electrician for the company
Changing the agreed design of a final circuit

questions.stem: The company brings in a new job-card app on the crew's phones. Some of the crew do not want to use it. What should the leader do?
options: Let those who dislike it keep using paper forms
Tell them it is not his decision, so there is nothing to discuss
Use it himself and fill in theirs for them
Explain why it is used, show them how, and help them start

questions.stem: Nordia is the only woman on a new crew, and some crew members make jokes about her. What should the leader do?
options: Laugh along so that the crew sees he is relaxed
Stop the jokes and make it clear everyone gets respect
Tell Nordia she must learn to ignore site jokes
Move Nordia to work alone where nobody bothers her

questions.stem: A client offers the crew cash to skip the insulation test so the job can finish early. What should the leader do?
options: Refuse politely and explain why the tests must be done
Take the cash and do the test later when there is time
Skip the test, because the client has accepted the risk
Ask the crew to vote on whether to do the test

questions.stem: Which helps a short site meeting work well?
options: Letting anyone talk for as long as they like
Holding it in a noisy area so that it stays short
A clear purpose, a few points and agreed actions
Leaving out the newest workers to save time

questions.stem: A client shouts at the leader about a delay caused by a late delivery. What is the best response?
options: Stay calm, listen, explain the cause and give a new date
Shout back so the client knows it was not his fault
Walk away and leave the crew to deal with the angry client
Say the delay is the supplier's problem, not his

questions.stem: The leader gave the crew the wrong cable size and they have pulled half the run. What should he do?
options: Tell the crew to carry on so no time is lost
Blame the stores clerk for giving out the wrong drum
Admit the error, stop the pull and plan the correction
Keep quiet and change the drawing to match the cable

questions.stem: How should a leading hand share out tasks in a crew of four?
options: Give the newest person the most work to toughen him up
Give each person the same task every day without change
Let the crew choose their own tasks each morning
Match tasks to skill, and give each person room to learn

questions.stem: An apprentice tells the leader that a stepladder has a cracked rail. What should the leader do?
options: Tell the apprentice to use it carefully and keep going
Take the ladder out of use, tag it and report it
Mark the crack with chalk so others can see it
Tape the crack and put the ladder back on the van

questions.stem: What should a crew leader put in a daily progress report to the supervisor?
options: Only the good news, so the supervisor is not worried
Work done, problems found, materials needed and plans
Each crew member's personal views about the company
A list of who the leader thinks should be let go

questions.stem: Which of these shows active listening when a crew member raises a problem?
options: Looking at them, asking questions, repeating the main point
Checking your phone while they talk so no time is wasted
Finishing their sentences to speed the talk along
Planning your reply while they are still talking

questions.stem: Which goal for the crew is written in the most useful way?
options: Work harder and do a better job this week
Try to finish the job sooner than last time
Fix all 40 outlet boxes on level 2 by Friday at 4 p.m.
Make the client happy with the work somehow

questions.stem: Who is accountable for making sure a delegated task is done correctly?
options: Only the worker who was given the task
The client, who will check it at handover
The supplier who sold the materials used
The leader who delegated it, and the worker too

questions.stem: Andre is not the leading hand, but he is the crew's most experienced electrician. How can he best support leadership?
options: Give the crew his own orders whenever he disagrees
Stay out of all decisions so that he is never blamed
Back the leader's plan and offer his ideas to the leader
Wait for the leader to make mistakes and report them

questions.stem: A usually cheerful crew member has become quiet and is making mistakes. What should the leader do?
options: Give her harder work to keep her mind busy
Tell the crew to watch her work for mistakes
Report her to the manager for poor performance
Ask her privately if she is all right, and listen

questions.stem: Where would a crew leader find the company's rules on behaviour, safety and the use of company vehicles?
options: In the cable maker's data sheet
In the company's policies and procedures
On the title block of the client's drawing
In the wholesaler's tool catalogue

questions.stem: A new worker joins the crew on a hospital job. What should the leader make sure happens on his first day?
options: A site induction: hazards, rules, exits and who to ask
He works alone on day one so that he learns the job faster
He reads the company history before touching a tool
He shadows the hospital's staff instead of the crew

questions.stem: The crew keep running out of cable ties in the middle of a shift. What is the best long-term fix?
options: Tell the crew to use fewer ties on each run
Send someone to the hardware store each time
Ask the client to supply the cable ties for the rest of the job
Work out the usage and keep a minimum stock on the van

questions.stem: Why should a leader ask the crew for feedback on how a finished job went?
options: So the crew can be blamed for the parts that went wrong
To learn what to keep and what to change next time
Because the manager will not read the report otherwise
So the leader can avoid writing a job report at all

questions.stem: Which is a fair way to give out overtime?
options: Offer it in turn from a clear, open list
Give it to the leader's friends first
Give it only to those who never complain
Give it to whoever asks the loudest

questions.stem: A client asks the leading hand for two extra circuits that are not in the contract. What should he do?
options: Fit the extra circuits and charge the client in cash
Refuse rudely and tell the client to read the contract
Note the request and pass it to the supervisor to agree
Fit them free of charge to keep the client happy

questions.stem: Which is the best way for a new leading hand to improve his leadership skills?
options: Copy whatever the loudest supervisor on site does
Avoid hard decisions until he has more years in the job
Ask for feedback, learn from a mentor, do short courses
Wait for the company to tell him what he does wrong

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the short meeting at the start of a shift, where the crew hear the tasks and hazards for the day, usually called?
What word means giving a task, and the authority to do it, to another person while you stay accountable for it?
What is the written set of rules called that tells staff how they are expected to behave at work?
In the SMART way of setting goals, what does the letter T stand for?
What is it called when a worker's private interests could affect a decision they make for their employer?
What is an experienced worker called who guides and advises a less experienced worker over a long period?
What kind of listening means giving full attention, asking questions and repeating back the main points?
Which form must be filled in when a crew member is hurt on the job, however small the injury?
Who does a leading hand normally pass a decision to when it is outside their own authority?
What is the meeting after a job called, where the crew talk about what went well and what to improve?
What word means being honest and keeping to strong moral principles, even when nobody is watching?
What is feedback called that praises good work in order to encourage more of it?
Besides a tag, what does each worker fit to the isolating switch, keeping its key, during safe isolation?
How many people should hold the key to a worker's personal safety padlock?
What is the chart called that shows tasks as bars along a time scale, to plan who does what and when?

essays.stem: Explain how a leading hand on an electrical crew can model high standards of work and behaviour. Give four examples and say why each one matters to the crew.
essays.modelAnswer: A leading hand teaches more by what he does than by what he says. First, he follows safe isolation every time: switch off, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked before and after. If he skips it, the crew will think it is optional. Second, he wears the right PPE and keeps his tools and test instruments in good order, so the crew see that standards apply to everyone. Third, he arrives on time, starts the toolbox talk on time and keeps his promises, which shows respect and builds trust. Fourth, his own work is neat and checked against the drawing and specification, so the crew know what good work looks like. He also speaks politely to clients and to the crew, owns up to his mistakes and treats everyone fairly. When the leader sets the example, the crew follow it, the company's image improves and the job is safer.
markingPoints: Explains that the crew copy the leader's behaviour
Safety example: safe isolation and PPE every time
Example of reliability: time keeping and keeping promises
Example of quality: neat work checked against drawings and specification
Example of conduct: respect, honesty, owning mistakes, with a reason for each

essays.stem: A crew member keeps skipping safe isolation to save time. Describe how you, as the crew leader, would deal with this now and over the following weeks.
essays.modelAnswer: Now, I stop the work at once, because someone could be killed. I have him switch off, lock off with his own padlock, tag the switch and prove the circuit dead with a tester that is checked on a proving unit before and after. Then I speak to him privately and calmly. I ask why he is skipping it: is it pressure to finish, a missing lock, or not knowing the steps? I explain the danger and the company rule, and I make it clear that it must not happen again. I record what happened and tell my supervisor, as the company procedure says. Over the next weeks I fix any cause, for example getting more padlocks and testers, or easing the time pressure. I use the next toolbox talk to remind the whole crew, without naming him. I check his work more often and praise him when he does it right. If he keeps breaking the rule, the matter goes to the supervisor for formal action.
markingPoints: Stops the work immediately and has the circuit safely isolated and proved dead
Talks privately and finds the reason
Records it and reports it to the supervisor as procedure requires
Fixes the cause (equipment, time pressure, training) and briefs the crew
Follows up: checks, praises good practice, escalates if it continues

essays.stem: The crew can either work late tonight to finish a shop rewire or come back tomorrow morning. Describe the steps you would follow to make an informed decision.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make clear what must be decided and by when. Then I gather the facts. How much work is left, and how long will it take? Is there enough light and are the crew tired, which raises the risk of mistakes and accidents? Does the shop owner need the power back tonight, and what does the contract say? Are materials and test instruments on site? What will overtime cost compared with another visit? Next I ask the crew for their views, because they know how tired they are and what is left. I list the options, with their good and bad points for safety, quality, cost and the client. Safety comes first: if the crew are too tired to work safely, we return. If the decision is outside my authority, such as paying overtime, I check with my supervisor. I then make the decision, explain it to the crew and the client, and record it. Afterwards I check whether it worked out.
markingPoints: Defines the decision and gathers facts (work left, time, client needs, cost)
Considers safety and fatigue first
Consults the crew
Compares options and checks limits of authority with the supervisor
Makes, explains, records and reviews the decision

essays.stem: Explain five ways a crew leader can build and keep the trust of the team.
essays.modelAnswer: Trust grows when the crew can rely on the leader. First, he keeps his word: if he says he will order more cable or ask about overtime, he does it, or he explains why he could not. Second, he is fair. He shares tasks, overtime and the dirty jobs evenly and does not have favourites. Third, he is honest. He tells the crew the truth about problems and admits his own mistakes instead of blaming others. Fourth, he keeps private matters private, such as a worker's health or family problems. Fifth, he backs his crew. He listens to their ideas and concerns, deals with them, and gives credit to the person who did the good work. He also takes their safety seriously, so they know he will never push them to cut corners. If trust is lost, it takes a long time to win back, so the leader must be consistent every day.
markingPoints: Keeps promises
Is fair and consistent, with no favourites
Is honest and admits mistakes
Keeps private information confidential
Listens, gives credit and protects the crew's safety

essays.stem: Describe how to delegate a task to a junior worker well. Include how you choose the task and the person, how you brief them and how you follow up.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose a task that the person can do with their training, or can learn safely with some help, and that is within my own authority to hand over. Tasks such as signing test certificates or agreeing prices stay with the right person. I pick the worker by matching the task to their skill and to what they need to learn next. When I brief them, I explain what the task is, why it matters, the standard I expect, the drawing or specification to follow, the hazards and controls, the tools and materials, and when it must be finished. I ask them to tell me back the main steps, and I tell them when and how to ask for help. I then let them get on with it, but I check at agreed points, early enough to catch mistakes. At the end I inspect the work, give feedback on what was good and what to improve, and record it. I stay accountable for the result.
markingPoints: Chooses a suitable task within authority, and the right person for it
Briefs clearly: what, why, standard, hazards, deadline
Checks understanding and tells them how to get help
Checks progress at agreed points without taking over
Inspects, gives feedback and stays accountable

essays.stem: Two crew members disagree strongly about how to run a cable route, and the argument is slowing the job. Describe how you would handle this conflict.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stop the argument in front of others and make sure the work is left safe. I take the two of them aside to a quiet place and let each one explain his view without being interrupted. I listen, ask questions and repeat back what I heard so they know I understood. I keep the talk on the work, not on the people. Then I look at the facts: the drawing, the specification, the distances, the number of bends, the cost and any safety issues. Often both have a good point, and the best answer takes something from each. If the facts are clear, I decide and explain why. If the matter is outside my authority, such as a change to the design, I ask the supervisor. I thank both for caring about the job, make sure they can work together, and record the agreed route. Later I check that the bad feeling has gone. If it carries on, I pass it to the supervisor.
markingPoints: Stops the argument and talks privately, keeping work safe
Lets each side speak and listens actively
Uses facts (drawings, specification, safety, cost) not personalities
Decides or escalates, and explains the decision
Records the outcome and follows up

essays.stem: Explain how a crew working in a client's occupied home can protect and improve the company's image. Give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: In someone's home the crew are the company's face. They arrive on time, in clean work clothes with ID if the company gives it, and they greet the client politely. The leader explains what will happen that day, how long the power will be off and which rooms they need. The crew protect the home: dust sheets over furniture, mats at the door, and vacuuming of drill dust. They keep the work area tidy and tools out of reach of children. They do not use the client's things without asking, they do not smoke or play loud music, and they speak respectfully, with no bad language. They keep the client's details and the layout of the home private. At the end the leader shows the client the finished work, explains any switches or labels, and leaves the place clean, with all waste taken away. If something goes wrong, he apologises and puts it right quickly. This brings repeat work and good word of mouth.
markingPoints: Punctual, tidy appearance, polite greeting
Explains the day's work and power cuts to the client
Protects and cleans the home
Respectful behaviour and confidentiality
Good handover and quick, honest handling of problems

essays.stem: Compare positive feedback and corrective feedback. Describe how to give each one so that the worker improves.
essays.modelAnswer: Positive feedback tells a worker what they did well, so they keep doing it. Corrective feedback tells them what must change and how. Both should be specific, timely and about the work, not the person. For positive feedback I say exactly what was good and why it matters, for example: Kimone, your labels on that board are clear and match the circuit chart, which will save time at testing. Praise can be given in front of the crew. Corrective feedback is given privately and soon after the event. I describe what I saw, explain the effect, and ask the worker for their view. Then we agree what to do and I offer help, such as showing the method again. I finish on a positive note and check later that the change has been made. Feedback that is vague, too late or given in anger does not help. A good leader gives much more positive than corrective feedback, so the crew trust it.
markingPoints: Defines both kinds correctly
Both specific, timely and about the work
Positive: names what was good and why; can be public
Corrective: private, describes the effect, agrees a fix and offers help
Follows up and keeps a good balance of praise

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and deliver a ten-minute toolbox talk on the first morning of a new job.
essays.modelAnswer: I plan it the day before. I read the drawings, the job plan and the risk assessment, and I list the tasks for the day and who will do each one. I note the main hazards, such as live parts nearby, ladders, drilling dust and heat, and the controls for each, especially safe isolation with lock, tag and a tester checked before and after. I add the emergency points: first-aid kit, nearest hospital, assembly point and who to call. I keep it short with a few key points. On the morning I hold the talk at the work area, where everyone can hear and see. I speak plainly, show any equipment, and ask questions to check understanding, for example asking someone to tell the group how to prove dead. I invite the crew to raise their own concerns. Everyone signs the attendance sheet. Afterwards I deal with any concerns and keep the record with the job file.
markingPoints: Prepares from drawings, job plan and risk assessment
Covers tasks, roles, hazards and controls including safe isolation
Includes emergency information
Delivers clearly and checks understanding with questions
Invites concerns and keeps a signed record

essays.stem: The company has changed its rules for working at height. Explain how you would introduce the change to your crew and check that it is followed.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure I understand the new rules myself, and I ask my supervisor about any part that is unclear. I check what the change means for our job: perhaps we now need a mobile platform instead of a stepladder for ceiling work, or a second person to foot ladders. I make sure the equipment is on site before the change starts. Then I explain the change at a toolbox talk: what is changing, why the company made the change, and what each person must do. I show the equipment and how to use it, and I let the crew ask questions and raise concerns. I give the new rules out in writing and have the crew sign that they were briefed. From that day I follow the rules myself, every time. I check the work areas each day, correct anyone who slips back politely but firmly, and praise those who follow the rules. I report problems with the new rules to my supervisor.
markingPoints: Understands the change and gets the equipment ready
Explains what, why and how at a briefing
Lets the crew ask questions; records the briefing
Leads by example
Checks, corrects, praises and reports problems upward

practical1.title: Plan and deliver a pre-start briefing for a new electrical job
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a job card: a three-day rewire of a small shop in Spanish Town, with the shop's owner wanting power back each evening. As a group, plan a ten-minute pre-start briefing (toolbox talk) for the first morning. On a briefing sheet, write the tasks for day one and who does each, the main hazards and their controls (safe isolation with lock, tag and a tester checked before and after; ladders; drilling dust; working in an occupied shop), the emergency arrangements, and three questions to check understanding. Split the briefing into sections and give each member one section to lead. Then deliver the briefing as a role play to the assessor and the other groups, who act as the crew. Each leader asks at least one question to check understanding and records any concerns raised. Finish by completing an attendance sheet and a short review: what went well and what the group would change.
materials: Job card for the shop rewire (from the assessor)
Blank briefing sheet, attendance sheet and review sheet
Sample risk assessment and site rules
Flip chart or whiteboard and markers
A padlock, tag and voltage tester to show during the talk (not connected to anything)
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The group planning, with roles written up on the flip chart
Each member leading their section of the briefing
The lock, tag and tester being shown to the crew
The signed attendance sheet with concerns recorded
checklist: Took a full part in planning the briefing
Named the hazards in their section and gave correct controls
Spoke clearly and kept to time
Asked a question to check understanding and dealt with the answer
Recorded concerns raised by the crew and said what would be done
Gave the safe isolation steps correctly where they came up
Contributed to the review with a practical improvement
safety: This is a classroom role play: no electrical work is done
Any tester or padlock shown is not connected to a supply
Keep walkways clear of bags and flip-chart stands

practical2.title: Lead a team decision and handle workplace issues by role play
practical2.brief: Part A (decision): the assessor tells the group that the cable for a hotel job in Ocho Rios will arrive three days late, and the handover is on Friday. As a group, list at least three options, score them on a decision sheet for safety, quality, cost, time and the client, and agree a choice. Write a short decision record and a message to the supervisor that explains the choice and asks for anything outside the leading hand's authority. Part B (role plays): the assessor gives five scene cards: a worker skipping lock-off, two workers arguing over clean-up, an apprentice whose conduit is not level, a client complaining about dust, and a supplier offering a gift. Each member plays the leading hand in one scene while the others play the other parts and one member observes and writes notes on the scene sheet. Rotate until everyone has led a scene. Finish with a five-minute debrief.
materials: Scenario sheet for the late delivery (from the assessor)
Blank decision sheet, decision record and message form
Five scene cards and an observer's note sheet for each scene
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The list of options on the flip chart
The completed decision sheet with scores
The decision record and the message to the supervisor
Each role-play scene, with the scene card in view
The observer's notes for each scene
checklist: Helped list options and gave reasons when scoring them
Kept safety first and recognised what needed the supervisor's approval
As leading hand in a scene, stayed calm and listened before acting
Dealt with the scene in line with safety rules, ethics and company policy
Spoke respectfully and agreed a clear next step
As observer, wrote fair and specific notes
safety: This is a classroom role play: no electrical work is done
Role plays stay respectful: no shouting at or touching another person
Photos show the scene and notes; nobody is photographed without agreeing
